name: Phloretin

card.summary: An apple-tree polyphenol used in antioxidant serums, studied for photoaging protection and for evening out pigmentation.
card.note: Skin penetration profile across layers has not been fully characterised.

quick.overview:
Phloretin is a dihydrochalcone, a natural phenol found in apple tree leaves and the Manchurian apricot. In cosmetics it is used as an antioxidant ingredient, for firmer, more even-toned skin.
A 2020 review describes dermatological work on melasma, photoaging, acne and melanoma, reporting that phloretin inhibited elastase and matrix metalloproteinase-1 and lowered tyrosinase activity and melanin content in lab studies.
quick.how: It is applied topically in serums. The review notes it can penetrate skin, though its distribution through skin layers was not yet established.
quick.risks: Human safety data for topical phloretin is limited; most mechanistic findings come from cell and animal studies.

lead: Phloretin is a dihydrochalcone, a type of natural phenol with the formula C15H14O5, found in apple tree leaves and the Manchurian apricot (Prunus mandshurica).[1]

In skin care it has drawn interest as an antioxidant and as a depigmenting agent. A 2020 European Journal of Pharmacology review covers use in melasma, photoaging, acne and melanoma, reporting that phloretin inhibited elastase and MMP-1 activity, reduced cellular tyrosinase activity and melanin content, and in mice suppressed induced COX-2 expression.[2]
It is also studied outside skin care: animal work shows it inhibits glucose transporters SGLT1 and SGLT2 and some urea transporters and aquaporin 9.[1]

chain: Less photoaging damage and pigment production in lab models
angle.text: Phloretin is used in serums for its antioxidant and depigmenting properties, based mostly on laboratory and animal findings.

paras: The 2020 review reports anti-aging and depigmenting properties, including inhibition of elastase and MMP-1 and reduced melanin content in cells; it notes that skin penetration across layers is not yet well characterised.[2]

Phloretin inhibits SGLT1 and SGLT2 glucose transporters less strongly than its glycoside phlorizin and inhibits several urea transporters; in rats phlorizin is converted to phloretin in the small intestine.[1]
No studies found. Laboratory and animal skin research is described in the 2020 review.[2]
